claims.text: The feedstock is AlCrFeNiSi powder with controlled spherical morphology and a particle-size distribution comparable to conventional AM powders.
The build platform should be preheated to 600–700 °C during additive manufacturing.
The intervention is applicable to laser powder bed fusion or a comparable additive-manufacturing process.
The applicable components have millimeter-scale dimensions.
The build should be conducted in an inert atmosphere.
Laser power, scan speed, and hatch distance should be held at otherwise conventional values while platform temperature is changed.
Build-platform preheating reduces thermal gradients during deposition.
Reduced thermal gradients lower the accumulation of residual dislocations.
More uniform cooling minimizes microcrack formation.
Elevated build-platform temperature reduces rapid contraction-induced stresses and enables more gradual solidification.
Preheating produces a refined microstructure with lower dislocation density and fewer stress-induced defects.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi components will have significantly lower residual stress than room-temperature-platform controls.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi components will have fewer microcracks than room-temperature-platform controls.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi components will exhibit greater ductility than room-temperature-platform controls.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi components will exhibit greater strength than room-temperature-platform controls.
Room-temperature build platforms produce high residual thermal stresses and degraded mechanical properties because of rapid cooling and high thermal gradients.
The intervention is expected to be most effective for miniature components, while larger builds may respond differently because of different heat-dissipation behavior.
The 600–700 °C processing window is based on analogous findings from other additive-manufacturing systems.
SEM, EBSD, and TEM can be used to characterize microstructure and defects in the fabricated specimens.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in residual stress and microcracking together with improved strength or ductility would falsify the hypothesis.
